paras: The assault on Arthur Glande was the beating of a Black man at Grand Bay, Alabama, in late August 1905, which he said was carried out by two young white men, August Fichet and Ashton Page, with persimmon limbs. The two men were charged with assault and released on bond, and a Mobile correspondent of the Montgomery Advertiser described the episode as "a peculiar story" because it grew out of a quarrel over race and kinship.

According to the account gathered from both the accused men and Glande, the three met at a charcoal kiln, where the white men had been invited to dinner by a friend. When Glande was also asked to dinner, Page and Fichet said they were from Mississippi and did not "eat with niggers," and Glande objected.

In the argument that followed, Page said that he and Fichet were related to the Ladniers, and Glande answered that he was kin to the same family. The white men took this to mean that they had "negro blood in their veins." They left, and, as Glande claimed, later met him and beat him severely with persimmon limbs. The report gives no date for the beating and no description of his injuries beyond his own statement.

Sheriff Powers and Deputy Sheriff Charley Cherry brought Fichet and Page from Grand Bay to Mobile on the morning of the report, charged with assault. After arriving, the two gave bond for their appearance in the Inferior Criminal Court; no report of a hearing or trial was found.

The only report found was a short Mobile item on page 3 of the Montgomery Advertiser of August 31, 1905. Written in a neutral tone, it printed the white men's slur in quotation marks, attributed the beating to Glande's claim, and treated the case as a curiosity rather than as a crime of note. No coverage of the episode in the Black press was found.
